e.t: This Greek Old Testament word means the bend of the arm—the elbow. It is a noun naming a specific part of the human body, rather than an action or figurative quality. Within the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs six times, including references in 2 Chronicles, Job, Ezekiel, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning remains the elbow or the arm’s joint.

This Greek LXX noun means “fault” or “case.” It can name a fault being identified or a case being considered. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence presents the fault or case, but its central meaning remains a matter identified for attention or consideration.

This noun refers to an “avenging deity” or “destroying angel”—a supernatural figure associated with bringing destructive judgment or vengeance. The wording presents the figure by its action and role, not as a general word for any person who takes revenge. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical writings: once in 2 Maccabees and three times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

Amon is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Amon” and is not presented here with a descriptive definition beyond the name itself. This word occurs 14 times in 14 Old Testament verses, beginning in 2 Kings 21:18 and continuing through Zephaniah 1:1. Because it is a personal name, its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

This verb means to unsettle—to disturb, disrupt, or make something unstable. It describes an action that shakes an established condition rather than leaving it secure and orderly. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Daniel 7:23, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains clear: to unsettle something is to disturb its stability or established arrangement. The word is a verb, expressing what someone or something does.

This verb means to “keep off” or “ward off”—to prevent something from reaching or affecting someone. It describes an act of resisting, blocking, or holding back a threat or unwanted force. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:19. The exact force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This verb means “kick off,” describing the act of driving something away with a kick. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy 32:15. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself presents a forceful kicking away or rejection.

Araël, also rendered Arel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named person or place in the biblical record. This name occurs once, in Joshua 19:36. The available rendering is Arael, while the lexical definition gives the approved forms “Araēl; Arel.” Its precise referent must be identified from the surrounding passage, since the name itself does not state a broader meaning.

“Arthasastha” is a proper name—the personal designation rendered as Arthasastha in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a name used in the Ezra–Nehemiah material. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 14 verses, from Ezra 4:7 through Nehemiah 13:6. Its precise identification and role in any particular verse require that verse’s surrounding text.

This noun refers to a person who ploughs land or works as a husbandman. Its central idea is an agricultural worker involved in cultivating the soil. The word is rendered by the explicit meanings “plougher” and “husbandman,” which describe the same kind of rural laborer. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Isaiah 61:5. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular role or significance of that person there; the word itself identifies the worker by his agricultural occupation.

This verb means “rule” or “begin.” It can describe exercising authority over others, or the start of an action, period, or event. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 128 times, showing that both senses belong to its normal use. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on governing or on commencing something. Its use ranges across historical, legal, prophetic, and narrative passages. Scripture references include Genesis 1:18, Deuteronomy 1:5, and 1 Samuel 9:17.

Asephērath, also given as Asefirath, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek LXX, at Ezra 2:55. Because it is a name and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its specific referent must be understood from that passage rather than from the name itself. The form identifies a named individual or entity in the biblical record.

Assa is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:33. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or theological idea; its role is to identify someone or somewhere in the biblical record. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what Assa refers to in that passage.

Aschazi, also rendered Askhazi, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, specifically in the book of Judges. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Judges 1:31. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name itself does not provide a broader meaning beyond identifying the person it names.

Achel, also called Akhel, is a proper name used to identify a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The available meaning is the name itself rather than a descriptive word for an action, quality, or object. This LXX word appears twice, once in Joshua and once in 1 Kings. The surrounding verse text would be needed to determine which person or location each occurrence identifies.

Baithsan is a proper name for a place, also rendered Vethsan. It is not a general description or action but a geographic name used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings. The name occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages in Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the place known by these two forms.

Baisaphoud is a proper name, also rendered “Vesafuth.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:12. The available information establishes the name and its single occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person or place it identifies.

The word means “firm.” It is an adjective used to describe something as firm rather than naming an action or event. In the Greek Old Testament/LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, across Esther, Wisdom, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Because verse texts are not provided, its precise force in each occurrence must be determined from its surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name, preserved in English as “Bērbēthnema” or “Virvithnema.” It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word or action word, so its name alone does not explain what a reader should believe or do. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:10. Understanding its precise reference requires the verse and surrounding passage, which identify how the name functions there.

This noun means pain: suffering or distress experienced by a person. It identifies what hurts or causes anguish rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:9. The word’s central idea remains straightforward—pain itself—while the surrounding verse would determine whether the reference is bodily, emotional, or figurative in that setting. As a noun, it names the experience rather than expressing an action or command.

“Gaienna” or “Yeenna” is a proper name, identifying a particular named person, place, or thing rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 18:16. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its specific referent cannot be identified more precisely from this word alone. The two supplied forms are alternate English representations of the same name in this LXX passage.

This word is the proper name “Gebal,” also given as “Yeval.” In the Greek Old Testament, it functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once, in Psalm 82:8, and its English rendering there is “Gebal.” Because it is a proper name with a single occurrence, its central meaning is simply the identification of the named entity in that passage.

This word means “tenth,” describing the person, thing, or portion that comes in position ten or represents one part out of ten. It is an adjective, so it identifies an ordinal position rather than simply naming a quantity. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 64 times, often in language involving numbered portions, offerings, measurements, or ordered times. Its basic meaning remains consistent: something is tenth because it holds the tenth place or amounts to a tenth portion.

This adjective describes something public or provided at the public cost. It points to a matter associated with the community’s shared resources rather than a private expense. As an adjective, it qualifies a noun by marking its public character or funding. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:1. The precise application there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a monetary amount of “hundred dollars.” In the Greek Old Testament, it names a measured sum of money rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs 26 times across 19 verses, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a monetary amount valued at one hundred dollars.

This word means “therefore in fact,” joining a statement to what follows with a strong sense of consequence or confirmation. It can point to a conclusion while also stressing that the conclusion truly follows. As a conjunction and adverb, it helps connect reasoning rather than naming a person, action, or object. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs five times, all in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence is shaped by the surrounding words.

This Greek LXX verb means “catch,” describing the act of taking hold of someone or something. It presents catching as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, appearing in passages from Leviticus, Numbers, Psalms, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on what is being caught and the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the active taking or seizing of something.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “cast out” or “divorce,” describing the act of sending someone away, especially in the context of a marriage. It functions as an action word rather than a title or description of a person. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in two passages from Leviticus and one from Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is dismissal or the ending of a marital union.

This verb means to convict someone—showing that a person is guilty or in the wrong—or to question someone in a searching, examining way. Its two related senses involve bringing a matter into the open: wrongdoing may be exposed and answered for, or a person may be challenged to respond. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 53 times, so its precise force depends on whether the sentence concerns guilt or serious questioning.

Elisae is a personal name, used to identify a particular person rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. It is a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). This name occurs once in that corpus, at 1 Chronicles 14:5. The name itself gives the person’s designation, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain anything further about that individual or the role the name has in that specific setting.

This LXX word means “next to; before,” describing position in space, presence before someone, or a place in front of something. As an adverb or preposition, it can mark where someone or something is located or whom they face. It occurs 412 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, and “before” is its usual English rendering. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means “extract” or “take out.” It describes removing something or someone from a place or situation. As a verb, it focuses on the action of bringing out, drawing out, or taking away rather than on the object itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 132 times, showing that this is a commonly used action word across the corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “astonish” or “beside yourself.” It describes a person whose reaction is so strong that he is overwhelmed, startled, or no longer acting with ordinary composure. As a verb, it expresses the act or state of becoming astonished rather than naming a person or object. It occurs 66 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing that it is used across many Old Testament and related Greek writings to describe intense astonishment or disorientation.

This Greek LXX verb means “survive”: to remain alive or continue living through a circumstance that could have ended life. It describes an action or condition rather than a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, once in Genesis and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on living beyond a danger, hardship, or expected end; the surrounding verse determines what circumstance the survival concerns.

This noun means “longing; aspiration”: a strong desire directed toward something a person wants or hopes for. It can describe an inward yearning, whether the desire is focused on people, possessions, experiences, or a hoped-for outcome. The word appears 69 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it covers a broad range of desire rather than one narrow emotion. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what the person longs for.

This Greek LXX adverb means “carefully,” describing action carried out with attention and deliberate thoroughness. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent across several settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains acting with care instead of haste or neglect.

gl: in possession of his rights and franchises
d: in possession of his rights and franchises

e.t: This adjective describes someone who is “in possession of his rights and franchises.” It refers to a person recognized as having the rights or privileges belonging to him, rather than being deprived of them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is established legal or personal entitlement.

This adjective describes someone or something that can be taken easily—readily seized, captured, or brought under another’s control. Its central idea is vulnerability to being taken rather than strength or resistance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:28, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s plain sense remains “easy to be taken,” describing something accessible to capture or possession.

This Greek verb means “stand over/by” or “get attention.” It describes someone positioning themselves nearby or standing over another person, and it can also express drawing notice. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 68 times, showing that it is used across many passages for an action of standing near, appearing, or making oneself noticed. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and scene.

Zemma is a proper name, preserved in English as “Zemma.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:5. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that genealogy must be understood from the context of the passage itself.

This word means “half”: one of two equal parts of a whole, or an amount that is half as much. As an adjective, it describes a portion, measure, quantity, or share rather than naming the whole thing itself. Its central idea is division into two corresponding parts. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 129 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for describing partial amounts and portions. The same basic meaning applies whether it describes part of an object, a quantity, or a share.

Thalcha, also written Thalkha, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek text, at Joshua 19:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise referent cannot be described further without adding information beyond the name itself.

This noun means “beast,” referring to an animal. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for animals in ordinary descriptions and narratives, including creatures associated with the earth, human life, and danger. The word occurs 75 times across 73 verses, so it has a broad animal-related use rather than pointing to one particular species. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Iais,” also given as “Ies.” It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:39. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that genealogy must be understood from that passage itself. Its basic lexical meaning is therefore the personal name “Iais” or “Ies.”

Iespha, also rendered Iesfa, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:16. Because this name occurs only in that genealogical setting and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its lexical meaning is simply the person’s name; the reference identifies where that person is mentioned, not an additional meaning for the name.

This word is a proper personal name, represented by the forms “Iōzabed” and “Iozaveth.” It does not function as a general description or action word, but identifies an individual by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 24:26. The available information establishes the name’s identity and use as a designation, but does not provide a broader lexical meaning or etymological explanation.

This word means “folly,” describing foolish or senseless thinking and behavior. It is a noun, so it names this condition rather than presenting an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 16:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, but its central sense remains folly: a lack of sound judgment that leads a person away from wisdom. The word’s definition is brief, yet clear, and points to foolishness as a recognizable condition rather than a passing mistake.

Karia is a proper name identifying a specific person, place, or entity named in the text. The word itself does not describe an action, quality, or relationship; it functions as a name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, Karia occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 15:23. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the exact person or location to which the name refers cannot be identified from the name alone.

This verb means “proclaim”: to announce or declare something openly. It describes an act of making a message known rather than merely thinking or speaking privately. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains public announcement or declaration. The word is therefore used for communicating a message clearly and openly to others.

This verb means “spread out over,” describing something being extended across or covering an area. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:8, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This LXX Greek verb means “press down; depress.” As a verb, it describes the act of pushing something downward or causing it to be lowered. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Exodus 22:24. The word itself gives the basic action, while the sentence around it determines what is being pressed down and how the action functions in that passage.

This Greek Old Testament word means “scorching heat.” It is a noun describing intense, burning heat rather than a person, action, or abstract quality. In the Septuagint, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including passages from Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Sirach. Its use can refer to heat experienced in the natural world, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding words and imagery.

This noun refers to brushwood or fagot-wood—small branches or sticks gathered as fuel. It names combustible wood rather than a living tree or a finished object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its basic meaning remains practical and material: wood collected or arranged for burning. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the gathered branches themselves or their use as fuel.

“Moulding” refers to a shaped ornamental feature, usually added as a raised or bordered part of an object or structure. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun appears three times, all in Exodus 25. It names a crafted detail rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. Its exact appearance and purpose in each occurrence must be understood from the surrounding description.

Laad, also written Laath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:2. The available information identifies the name and its rendering, but does not include the verse text or surrounding context needed to say more about the person named there. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Laad or Laath.

This word means “with the foot.” It is an adverb, so it describes an action as being done by means of, or with, the foot rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a foot-related manner of action.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “band of robbers”—a group identified by its unlawful, plundering activity rather than as a single thief. It names a collective body, so the word points to several people acting together. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within 2 Chronicles, including 2 Chronicles 22:1 and 36:5. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a group of robbers.

The word means “winnower,” a noun naming someone or something connected with winnowing—separating grain from unwanted chaff. It is a specific term for the agent or instrument involved in that work, rather than a general word for grain or harvest. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears once, at Proverbs 20:26; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use there.

This word means “softly.” As an adverb, it describes an action carried out in a quiet, gentle, or non-forceful manner. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 40:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is a soft or gentle manner of acting.

Macharim is a proper name, rendered “Macharim” or “Makharim.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 15:31. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be described further without speculation. The name itself is therefore best understood simply as Macharim, a proper designation preserved in the biblical text.

This Greek LXX verb means “in the middle,” describing something situated or occurring between other things. It points to a position within an interval or central part rather than to an action with a broad range of meanings. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 18:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic idea is being midway or centrally placed.

This verb means to commit adultery: to violate the marriage bond through sexual unfaithfulness. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twelve times, chiefly in passages addressing Israel’s covenant unfaithfulness or the command against adultery. Its central meaning remains direct and consistent wherever it occurs: adultery is treated as a serious breach of the relationship that marriage establishes. The word is found in eleven Old Testament occurrences and once in the Deuterocanonical books.

This noun describes someone who eats alone or is gluttonous. It points either to solitary eating or to excessive self-indulgence in food, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:7. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the exact emphasis in that occurrence cannot be determined from the word alone. Its central meaning remains a person characterized by eating alone or by gluttony.

Mōdad, also rendered Mothath, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 11, referring to the same named person. The name itself carries no further definition in the available lexical information, so its meaning is its role as a personal name. Its two occurrences are Numbers 11:26 and 11:27.

Naphisaios, also rendered Nafiseos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 5:19. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name alone does not tell us whom it identifies or what role that person has in the passage. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context of that verse.

Neserach, also rendered Neserakh, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 19:37. Since it is a personal or proper name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it names Neserach. The name’s significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “carrying wood,” referring to the act or duty of transporting pieces of wood. It names a practical activity rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 10:35. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the carrying or transporting of wood. This is a specific, concrete term describing physical work involving wood.

This noun means “weight,” referring to something measured by how heavy it is. It is used for physical weights in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, especially in passages that list measured offerings or valuable objects. The word occurs 24 times in the LXX corpus, so its basic sense is established across repeated descriptions of weighed items rather than a single isolated use. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to roam the mountains—to move about through mountainous places rather than remain in one location. It describes an action or activity, not a person, object, or fixed place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:15. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided, the word’s broader purpose in that sentence cannot be described responsibly. Its central meaning remains clear: traveling or wandering through the mountains.

This Greek LXX noun means “play; sport.” It refers to recreational or playful activity rather than work or serious obligation. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, showing a focused but recognizable meaning connected with games or amusement. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains an activity undertaken for play or sport.

“Ensign” describes something that serves as a distinctive sign or identifying mark. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person or thing by its sign-like, identifying role rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 2:29. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “own country,” referring to the land or homeland a person regards as their own. It can describe a person’s native place in contrast with another land or people. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 23 times, including passages from Leviticus, Esther, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books. Its basic sense remains focused on belonging to a particular country or homeland, while the surrounding passage determines the precise personal or national emphasis.

This Greek LXX verb means “survive”: to remain alive or continue living through danger, hardship, or a threatening situation. It describes what happens when someone lives through circumstances that could have ended life. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:18. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, the specific force of the word in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic meaning is to survive.

This Greek LXX verb means “go round” or “survive.” It can describe continuing to exist or remaining alive, while “go round” expresses movement around or through something. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Job, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is continued movement or continued life.

This Greek LXX word means “bird,” referring to a flying creature. It can function as a noun when naming the creature itself and can also describe something associated with birds. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times: once in Isaiah and twice in Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains straightforward; the surrounding verse determines how it functions in that passage. It is therefore a simple word for a bird or birds, without requiring an added figurative meaning.

This word means “faith” or “belief”: a noun describing trust or confidence. In the Greek Old Testament, it can name the quality of relying on someone as trustworthy or holding something to be true. Its central idea is inward confidence expressed toward a person, promise, or claim. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages translated with “faith.” Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic meaning remains faith or belief.

This adjective describes someone who has gained extensive experience and knows matters through repeated exposure or practice. It presents a person as highly seasoned rather than inexperienced, making it useful for describing a well-tested level of knowledge or skill. In the Greek of the Septuagint, it occurs three times, all in Sirach. The exact shade of meaning in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains someone deeply experienced.

This Greek LXX verb means “multiply; make numerous.” It describes increasing the number of people or things, so its basic idea is growth in quantity or population. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 32:13. Because no verse text is provided here, the surrounding passage determines exactly what is being multiplied in that occurrence. The word itself focuses on becoming many or causing something to become many, rather than on a particular method or result.

This noun means a means of approach or access. It refers to the way by which someone comes near or gains entry, whether understood as an approach or an available means of reaching something. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Joshua 15:7. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains an avenue, route, or means of access.

This word means “slap”: to strike someone with an open hand. It is a verb, describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Judges and once in Hosea. These references show that the word belongs to ordinary language for a physical blow, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains direct and concrete: delivering a slap or striking with the hand.

This Greek LXX noun means “lane,” referring to a route or way through which people move. It names a physical part of a town or settlement rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Isaiah and once in Sirach. Its basic meaning remains concise and concrete, while the surrounding verse determines what kind of lane or setting is intended. It is distinctively a place-word describing a passage used for movement.

gl: triangular musical instrument with four strings
d: triangular musical instrument with four strings

e.t: This word refers to a triangular musical instrument with four strings. It is a noun naming a specific instrument rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 3:5. The term identifies one of the instruments mentioned in that passage, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the instrument’s particular role in the scene.

This Greek LXX pronoun means “of yourself.” It refers back to the person being addressed, showing that something belongs to, concerns, or comes from that person rather than someone else. As a pronoun, it normally points to the addressee within a sentence and depends on surrounding words for its precise role. It occurs 223 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a regularly used way of expressing personal reference. The same basic idea remains whether the sentence speaks about a person’s actions, possessions, or concerns.

Sechenias, also rendered Sekhenias, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a word describing a quality, action, or object; its function is to name an individual. The name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Ezra, at Ezra 8:5 and Ezra 10:2. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not explain its etymology or the particular role of the person in either passage.

This LXX noun means “snare”—something that catches or entangles. It names a danger or trapping device rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including Leviticus, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, Psalms, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This adjective describes something fit for sowing, especially grain or a field intended for growing seed. It points to agricultural usefulness: land or material suitable for planting and producing crops. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs only twice, in Genesis and Leviticus, where its meaning remains connected with what can properly receive or support seed. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is suitability for sowing or association with a grain field.

This Greek LXX verb means to “laugh with sb,” describing the act of joining another person in laughter. It presents laughter as something shared with someone rather than merely directed at someone. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 30:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is clear: participating in another person’s laughter. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This adverb means “in harmony with” or “harmoniously with,” describing an action done in agreement, accord, or fitting unity with something else. It does not name a person or object; it tells how an action is carried out. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:6. The surrounding verse text is needed to see exactly what it modifies there, but its basic sense is coordinated, harmonious action rather than conflict or opposition.

This verb means to catch hold of something or someone. It describes the act of seizing or taking hold, rather than merely noticing or approaching. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs four times, including once in Proverbs and three times in 2 and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any passage depends on what is being grasped and the surrounding sentence.

This word refers to a meeting or assembly—a gathering of people who come together. As a noun, it names the gathering itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains focused on people gathered together, while the surrounding passage determines the particular circumstances of each gathering. The word is rendered “assembly” in one recorded English rendering, which agrees with its central meaning of a gathered meeting.

Sōb, also given as Sov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:40. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its particular family or narrative setting cannot be explained from the name alone. Its ordinary function is to identify the person who bears this name.

Sōpha, also rendered Sofa, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a person named Sōpha in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 7:35–36, and the supplied passages do not provide a broader lexical definition or explanation of the name’s meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 16, where the surrounding wording would determine exactly what object is being described. The word itself contributes the clear idea of hair being woven or arranged into the item. Its meaning remains specific and concrete, focused on appearance or workmanship.

This Greek LXX verb means “happen to be” or “belong.” It describes something existing, being present, or belonging to someone or something, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses a state or condition rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 71 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its basic idea appears in varied settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This word means “highest” or “most high.” As an adjective, it describes something at the greatest height or rank; as a noun, it can refer to the one who is highest. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 106 times, showing a recurring expression for supreme elevation or status. It appears in Genesis, Psalms, Daniel, and other books, including passages where “Highest” serves as a title. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “courts,” referring to enclosed grounds or areas associated with a building or place. It occurs once in the Greek Septuagint corpus, at 2 Kings 23:11. The word therefore identifies a physical part of a place rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a court or enclosed area. The word’s definition is explicit, while no additional translation renderings are available to broaden or qualify this sense.

This adjective describes something made of brass, a metal used for objects, fittings, and equipment. It can identify the material of an item rather than describe an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, the word occurs 96 times, showing its regular use for material objects and, in some passages, figurative descriptions of hardness or strength. Its precise force in any verse depends on the object or person it describes.

The word is a proper name rendered “Chananitis” or “Khananitis.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, once in Genesis 46:10 and once in Isaiah 19:18. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular reference in each passage cannot be stated more precisely. Its basic meaning is therefore the named designation itself.

This noun refers to a person or thing treated as an object of mockery—something held up to ridicule or scorn. It names what mockery is directed toward, rather than the act of mocking itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 12:4. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: the one or thing made a target of derision.

This Greek LXX adjective means “cold,” describing something lacking warmth or having a low temperature. It functions as a straightforward descriptive word rather than naming an object, person, or action. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Proverbs and once each in Sirach and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means to beautify or adorn—to make something attractive or give it pleasing appearance. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being beautified in the sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 25:1. Its recorded meaning is therefore clear, though the surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific object and emphasis there.
